title: Spanish Proverbs (Refranes) and What They Mean

body_html:
Spanish proverbs, called refranes or, in Mexico, dichos, are part of everyday conversation in a way that English proverbs rarely are anymore. Grandparents use them to give advice, parents use them to make a point, and friends use them as jokes. Knowing them helps you understand far more than the words: a single refrán can carry a whole attitude toward work, love or family. Here are the Spanish proverbs I hear most, with literal translations, real meanings and the closest English equivalents.

Quick answer
  • Más vale tarde que nunca. Better late than never.
  • Dime con quién andas y te diré quién eres. You are the company you keep.
  • No hay mal que por bien no venga. Every cloud has a silver lining.
  • Spanish proverbs are often shortened: people say the first half and expect you to know the rest.
{{toc}}

Spanish proverbs about life and luck

  • No hay mal que por bien no venga.
    Literally: there is no bad that doesn’t come for good. Meaning: something good comes out of every misfortune. English: every cloud has a silver lining.
  • Al mal tiempo, buena cara.
    Literally: to bad weather, a good face. Meaning: stay positive when things go wrong.
  • Más vale tarde que nunca.
    Literally: better late than never. Meaning: the same as in English.
  • Poco a poco se va lejos.
    Literally: little by little you go far. Meaning: steady progress gets results. English: slow and steady wins the race.
  • Del dicho al hecho hay mucho trecho.
    Literally: from saying to doing there is a long way. Meaning: talk is easy; action is hard. English: easier said than done.
  • El que no arriesga, no gana.
    Literally: whoever doesn’t risk, doesn’t win. Meaning: English: nothing ventured, nothing gained.
  • Cada loco con su tema.
    Literally: each crazy person with their topic. Meaning: everyone has their own obsession. English: to each their own.

Spanish proverbs about work and effort

  • Al que madruga, Dios lo ayuda.
    Literally: God helps the one who gets up early. Meaning: English: the early bird catches the worm.
  • Camarón que se duerme se lo lleva la corriente.
    Literally: the shrimp that falls asleep is carried away by the current. Meaning: if you don’t pay attention, you’ll miss out. Very common in Mexico.
  • Quien mucho abarca, poco aprieta.
    Literally: whoever grabs a lot squeezes little. Meaning: if you take on too much, you won’t do any of it well. English: don’t bite off more than you can chew.
  • No dejes para mañana lo que puedes hacer hoy.
    Literally: don’t leave for tomorrow what you can do today. Meaning: the same as in English.
  • El que algo quiere, algo le cuesta.
    Literally: whoever wants something pays something for it. Meaning: English: no pain, no gain.

In Mexico you will often hear only the first half, Camarón que se duerme…, with a meaningful look. Everyone knows how it ends.

{{image:2}}

Spanish proverbs about people and relationships

  • Dime con quién andas y te diré quién eres.
    Literally: tell me who you walk with and I’ll tell you who you are. Meaning: people judge you by your friends.
  • Ojos que no ven, corazón que no siente.
    Literally: eyes that don’t see, heart that doesn’t feel. Meaning: what you don’t know can’t hurt you. English: out of sight, out of mind.
  • Perro que ladra no muerde.
    Literally: a dog that barks doesn’t bite. Meaning: people who threaten loudly rarely act. English: his bark is worse than his bite.
  • Cría cuervos y te sacarán los ojos.
    Literally: raise crows and they will peck your eyes out. Meaning: help ungrateful people and they will turn on you.
  • Más vale solo que mal acompañado.
    Literally: better alone than in bad company. Meaning: the same idea in English.
  • El hábito no hace al monje.
    Literally: the habit doesn’t make the monk. Meaning: English: don’t judge a book by its cover.

Spanish proverbs about money and caution

  • Más vale pájaro en mano que cien volando.
    Literally: a bird in the hand is worth more than a hundred flying. Meaning: English: a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush.
  • A caballo regalado no se le mira el diente.
    Literally: you don’t look at the teeth of a gifted horse. Meaning: English: don’t look a gift horse in the mouth.
  • En boca cerrada no entran moscas.
    Literally: flies don’t enter a closed mouth. Meaning: sometimes it is better to stay quiet.
  • Más sabe el diablo por viejo que por diablo.
    Literally: the devil knows more for being old than for being the devil. Meaning: experience is the best teacher.
  • Agua que no has de beber, déjala correr.
    Literally: water you won’t drink, let it run. Meaning: don’t get involved in what doesn’t concern you.
{{book:the-mind-lies}}

How Spanish speakers really use proverbs

Proverbs are not just for books. In many families, they are a way of giving advice without sounding bossy. A mother might answer her son’s complaint about a new job with Al mal tiempo, buena cara. A grandmother might greet a late guest with a smile and Más vale tarde que nunca.

They are also used for humor. Friends twist them into jokes: Al que madruga… le da sueño todo el día (Whoever gets up early… is sleepy all day). Recognizing the original is what makes the joke work.

When I translate, proverbs are among the hardest things to carry over. A literal translation keeps the image but loses the punch, while an English equivalent keeps the punch but loses the image. I explain this trade-off in {{link:literal-translation-mistakes-spanish|literal translation mistakes in Spanish}}.

A sample conversation

Abuela: ¿Por fin conseguiste trabajo, mijo?
Did you finally get a job, dear?

Diego: Sí, pero empiezo a las seis de la mañana.
Yes, but I start at six in the morning.

Abuela: Pues al que madruga, Dios lo ayuda.
Well, the early bird catches the worm.

Diego: Ya sé, abuela. Más vale eso que nada.
I know, Grandma. Better that than nothing.

{{image:3}}

Where to find more

The Instituto Cervantes maintains a free online collection of Spanish proverbs with meanings and equivalents in other languages, the Refranero multilingüe. It is a reliable place to check a saying you hear. For idioms rather than full proverbs, see {{link:english-idioms-in-spanish|English idioms in Spanish}} and {{link:spanish-animal-idioms|Spanish animal idioms}}.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

Spanish proverbs are a shortcut into how Spanish speakers think about life, work and family. Learn a handful, listen for them at the dinner table, and try one yourself when the moment is right. For more expressions, see my guide to {{link:spanish-slang|Spanish slang}}.

faq.q: What is the difference between a refrán and a dicho?
faq.a: Both are traditional sayings. Refrán is the general term; in Mexico, people usually call them dichos.

faq.q: What is the most common Spanish proverb?
faq.a: Among the most common are más vale tarde que nunca, al que madruga, Dios lo ayuda and dime con quién andas y te diré quién eres.

faq.q: Do young people still use proverbs?
faq.a: Yes, often with humor or in shortened form. Older relatives use them most.

faq.q: Should I translate Spanish proverbs literally?
faq.a: Use the English equivalent when one exists. A literal translation usually sounds strange.

questions.q: Más vale tarde que nunca means…
questions.explain: The same proverb exists in English.
